client: I've been really struggling since I graduated last May. I still don't have a job in my field, and watching everyone else from my graduating class move forward with their careers makes me feel like I'm falling behind or like there's something fundamentally wrong with me. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds really heavy — that quiet, persistent ache of feeling left behind, even when you're trying to hold it together on the outside. I notice there's a thought showing up that says something must be *fundamentally wrong with you*, and I'd gently invite us to examine that together, because struggling in a difficult job market is not the same as being broken. The fact that you showed up here, even with doubt that it would help, tells me there's still a part of you that's reaching for something better — and that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like there's some truth to that thought — like, if nothing was wrong with me, wouldn't I have figured this out by now? Everyone else in my graduating class seems to be landing jobs or at least moving forward, and I'm just... stuck. I guess I showed up here because I didn't know what else to do, not because I actually believe something is going to change.
therapist: Your words sound measured, but the way you're speaking — the pace, the pitch — tells me this is hitting much deeper than you might be letting on, like there's a real pain underneath that's hard to fully voice. That thought, "if nothing was wrong with me, I'd have figured this out by now," is worth slowing down on, because it assumes everyone else's path is a fair comparison to yours — and that's actually a thinking trap called **comparing your insides to other people's outsides**. What we see of others is usually just the highlight reel, not the full story, and "stuck" right now doesn't mean "broken forever."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about the comparison thing, and I get it intellectually, but it's hard to actually believe it in the moment when I'm scrolling through LinkedIn and seeing people my age getting promotions or starting families. Like, I know I'm probably not seeing the full picture, but my brain just goes straight to "they have it together and I don't." And honestly, the loneliness of feeling stuck like this is almost worse than the actual being stuck, because there's no one in my life I can really talk to about it without feeling like a burden.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with a kind of urgency in your voice — tells me this loneliness piece might actually be the rawest part of all of this, even more than the job search itself. That feeling of being a burden to the people you love is such a painful, isolating thought, and I want to gently name it as exactly that — a *thought*, not a fact, because the people who care about you likely want to be there for you more than you're allowing yourself to believe. You came here, you're talking, and that's already you beginning to chip away at that isolation — that's not nothing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like you're just... supposed to say that, you know? Like, that's the therapeutic thing to say. Because when I actually think about reaching out to my friends during all of this job stuff, I picture their faces going kind of tight, like they're trying to figure out how to respond, and that image alone makes me pull back every time.
therapist: That image you just described — your friends' faces going tight — that's so specific and vivid, and I wonder if that picture in your mind has become more powerful than any actual evidence of how they'd really respond. Your voice carries something that sounds like a quiet, braced kind of pain, like you've been holding this at arm's length for a long time to protect yourself from a rejection that may not even happen. And I want to acknowledge your skepticism about what I say too — that's fair — so rather than taking my word for it, what might it look like to gently test that image against reality, just once, with someone you trust?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, part of me knows you might be right that I've built this image up in my head. But the thing is, even thinking about "testing it" makes my chest tighten, because what if the image isn't wrong — what if I do tell someone how lonely I've been feeling and their face actually does go tight like that? I've been carrying this for so long that I'm not sure I could handle it if the fear turned out to be real.
therapist: The tightness in your chest, the speed in your voice right now — your whole system is bracing against that possibility, and that makes complete sense when you've been carrying something this heavy, alone, for this long. But I want to sit with what you just said — "I'm not sure I could handle it" — because that thought itself is worth examining, because you *have* been handling this, every single day, even when it's felt unbearable. What if we thought about this not as one big leap of vulnerability, but as something much smaller — not a full confession, just the tiniest crack in the door with someone safe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible. But even thinking about "a tiny crack" feels terrifying, because what if that tiny crack is enough for someone to see how much I've been struggling and they just... pull away? I've been alone with this for so long that I think I've actually started to believe that keeping it hidden is what's keeping people close to me.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me something really important just surfaced — this belief that *hiding* is what's holding your relationships together, that your pain is somehow the thing that would drive people away rather than bring them closer. That's such a lonely way to have to exist, essentially managing everyone else's comfort by disappearing your own struggle, and I want to gently name that this belief, as understandable as it is, has become its own kind of prison. What if the hiding isn't protecting the relationship — what if it's actually preventing the deeper connection you're so hungry for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows there's truth in it, but it also feels really risky to just... let people see the mess. Like, I've tried being honest before and it didn't go the way I hoped, so now I have this evidence in my head that opening up just makes things worse. It's not just a belief I invented out of nowhere, it feels like something I learned the hard way.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, with a kind of tightness in your voice — tells me this isn't abstract fear, this is something that actually hurt you, and I want to honor that completely rather than talk you out of it. You're right that this isn't a belief you invented — it came from something real, and that deserves to be taken seriously rather than explained away. And yet, I'm curious — that past experience, as painful as it was, was it with everyone, or with a specific person or moment, because one door closing hard doesn't mean every door opens the same way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It was specific people, yeah — my old friend group, the ones I thought I could trust completely. But here's the thing, Luna, it's happened more than once, so it's not like it was just one bad experience I can write off as a fluke. That's what makes it hard to believe the "not every door" thing — when the pattern keeps repeating, it starts to feel less like bad luck and more like something must be wrong with me.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're saying something that clearly carries so much weight, tells me this conclusion — that something must be wrong with *you* — has been sitting with you for a long time, quietly and painfully. I want to gently offer another possibility though: patterns of painful experiences can also tell us something about the *specific people* we chose, or the circumstances we were in, rather than a fixed flaw inside you. What if we got curious together about what those experiences had in common — not to excuse the hurt, but to see if the pattern points somewhere other than straight back at you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it's hard not to feel like I'm the common denominator in all of it. Like, if it keeps happening with different people, different friendships, different situations, how do I point the finger anywhere else? I guess I'm just scared that if we look at the pattern and it still leads back to me, then there's nowhere left to hide from that truth.
therapist: The urgency and intensity in your voice right now tells me that underneath this very logical-sounding argument is something that feels almost like a verdict you're bracing to receive — and I want to slow that down, because "I'm the common denominator" is not the same as "I'm the problem." Being the common denominator means you were *present*, but it doesn't tell us anything yet about what you brought, what others brought, or what you were each needing that wasn't available — and that's exactly what we'd be looking at together, not to find someone to blame, but to understand. And I want to name something gently: the fact that you're *scared* of what we might find tells me how much you've already been punishing yourself with this conclusion, and you deserve more than a trial where you're the only witness against yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this other part that just keeps coming back to the same thing — like, if it's not me, then what is it? Because I've gone over it so many times, all these friendships that just kind of faded or fell apart, and I can't point to one clear moment where someone else was obviously the problem. It almost feels safer to just accept that it's me, because at least then I have some control over it.
therapist: You just said something really profound — that blaming yourself feels *safer* because it gives you control — and your voice, quick and strained, tells me this isn't a casual observation, this is something you've been gripping tightly for a long time as a way to survive the uncertainty. That's actually a really human and understandable thing to do, because "I'm the problem and I can fix myself" feels more manageable than "sometimes relationships fade for reasons that are messy and no one's fault and I can't fully control that." But I want to gently ask — has accepting that it's you actually given you the control and relief you were hoping for, or has it just given you something to punish yourself with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
